case.case_title: M. N. D. Perera vs Balapatabendi, Secretary to the President and others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. (F.R.) No. 27/2002, decided on 8 September 2004

clause.text: No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was discriminated against on the basis of political opinion or other prohibited grounds by being excluded from covering the swearing-in ceremony at the President’s House, violating Article 12(2).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that the exclusion was due to political animosity or ill feeling towards him and his media organization, constituting discrimination prohibited under Article 12(2).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the exclusion was not discriminatory but based on the President’s discretion and security/logistical considerations, and that the petitioner had no right of access as the President’s House is not a public place.
key_facts: The petitioner and his crew were excluded while other media were allowed.
The President’s House is official residence and not generally accessible to the public.
The exclusion was on the President’s instruction, with no security threat alleged.
The petitioner’s media organization was identified as adversative by the President.
No invitation was extended to the petitioner or his crew.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court found that discrimination on grounds such as political opinion is prohibited under Article 12(2). The exclusion of the petitioner and his crew was based on political animosity and personal ill will, not on legitimate security or logistical grounds, thus constituting unlawful discrimination under Article 12(2).
reasoning.application_to_facts: The petitioner was singled out for exclusion despite complying with all procedures and no security threat. Other media were allowed, indicating selective discrimination. The court rejected the argument that the President’s House being a non-public place justified discrimination.
principles_established: Discrimination on political opinion is prohibited under Article 12(2).
Official acts motivated by personal or political animosity violate constitutional equality guarantees.
Access restrictions must be based on legitimate, verifiable grounds, not subjective or arbitrary reasons.
precedents_cited: Bernard Soysa and Others v AG (1991) Sri LR 56
Victor Ivan v Silva (1998) 1 Sri LR 340
Prabha Dutt v Union of India AIR (1982) SC 6
Visuvalingam and Others vs Liyanage and Others No (1) (1983) 1 Sri LR 203
Wijesuriya v The State IT NLR 25
Sunila Abeysekera v Ariya Rubasinghe Competent Authority and Others (2000) 1 Sri LR 314

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner was discriminated against on the basis of political opinion, violating Article 12(2), and that such discrimination was unlawful.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Compensation and costs were awarded to the petitioner as a remedy for the violation.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(2) was central to the court’s finding that the petitioner’s exclusion was discriminatory on prohibited grounds, specifically political opinion, which was a key basis for the court’s decision to grant relief.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was excluded on the President’s instruction due to political animosity, while other media were allowed, with no security threat alleged, constituting discrimination prohibited by Article 12(2).
